name: GE-Act 2.0
summary: Most world action models start from a large pretrained video generator and bolt an action head on. GE-Act 2.0 instead trains every generative and action component from scratch on manipulation data. It has three parts: a control-oriented autoencoder that compresses observations heavily while keeping what matters for actions and instructions; a single-step visual planner that predicts the whole future state in one pass rather than denoising a video; and an inverse dynamics model that reads actions off the predicted future. The planner and inverse dynamics model can be pretrained separately (the planner on action-free video), then trained jointly with KASO, a selection step that keeps only predicted futures consistent with the recorded actions. Pretrained checkpoints are evaluated with no per-task fine-tuning on 100 tasks across 20 skill groups, including held-out scenes, lighting and objects. Scaling co-training data from 300 to 30,000 hours lifted success from 17.1% to 44.1% on the AgiBot G1 suite and from 13.4% to 31.1% on G2, even though G2 was under 2% of the data.
innovation: Shows a world action model does not need an internet-video generator as its starting point; manipulation data alone suffices at 30k hours.
One-pass future prediction (no iterative video denoising) keeps planning cheap enough for control.
KASO filters imagined futures by consistency with real actions, so action-free and action-labelled data can be combined.
matters: One of the clearest published data-scaling curves for a world action model on real robots, with per-skill coverage strongly predicting zero-shot success (Spearman 0.85).
Evidence of cross-embodiment transfer: the G2 robot gained 17.7 points from data that was mostly from G1.
limits: Absolute zero-shot success is still under 50%.
No code or weights released; results are on AgiBot's own robots.
lineage: Second generation of the GE-Act policy inside AgiBot's Genie Envisioner world-model platform (2025).
